title: Why a predicate offence is the foundation of every money laundering case
p1:
Many people think money laundering is simply about hiding illegal money.

But there is a missing piece that decides whether a money laundering case can even exist: where did the money come from?
p2:
A common misconception is that suspicious transactions alone are enough to prove money laundering. They are not.

Every money laundering case starts with a predicate offence — the original crime that generated the illegal proceeds, such as fraud, corruption, theft, or drug trafficking.
p3:
Think of a predicate offence as the foundation of a building. Without it, there is no base for the money laundering allegation to stand on.

The surprising part? Investigators may spend significant time tracing the movement of money, but they must also establish the criminal source behind it.

The practical takeaway: following the money is only half the story. The other half is proving where that money began.
conclusion: If the original crime cannot be proven, should a money laundering charge still be able to succeed? What do you think?
